newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian T-bills open weaker, eye on upcoming data.
newsitem.headline: Canadian T-bills open weaker, eye on upcoming data.

text.p: Canadian T-bills opened weaker on Monday, amid softer U.S. and Canadian fixed-income markets and a weaker currency, with investors largely focused on key economic data out tomorrow, analysts said.

"The weakness that you're seeing in the bill market is consistent with weakness in fixed-income markets generally in North America," said Doug Sannuto, director of Canada cash markets with Bank of Montreal. "I would think we'd continue to see a weakish tone here going into the employment cost index."
Canada's three-month when-issued T-bill weakened to yield 3.29 percent from 3.26 percent at Friday's close.

Both Candian and U.S. fixed-income markets are focused on this week's U.S. employment cost, gross domestic product and payroll employment data. The reports are seen as a key indication of whether U.S. interest rates will rise further in the near future.

Canada's dollar opened softer on Monday on selling in Europe overnight after Canada set an official election date of June 2. Traders said the election is unlikely to have a dramatic near-term impact on financial markets because the ruling Liberal Party is such a clear front-runner and investors remain tightly focused on the U.S. rate situation.
In other prices, the six-month when-issued T-bill softened to yield 3.72 percent from 3.67 percent on Friday.
The one-year T-bill softened to yield 4.35 percent, from 4.28 percent on Friday.
The call loan rate traded at 3.05 percent, near the center of the Bank of Canada's 2.75-3.25 percent target range. ((Jeffrey Hodgson (416) 941-8105, e-mail: jeffrey.hodgson@reuters.com))
